title: WHY DID GOD ALLOW POLYGAMY IN THE OLD TESTAMENT? THE ANSWER MAY CHANGE THE WAY YOU READ THE ENTIRE BIBLE
paragraphs:
WHY DID GOD ALLOW POLYGAMY IN THE OLD TESTAMENT? THE ANSWER MAY CHANGE THE WAY YOU READ THE ENTIRE BIBLE
God permitted something He never presented as Eden’s ideal—and the broken marriages of Abraham, Jacob, David, and Solomon reveal a truth far more uncomfortable, and far more beautiful, than most people expect.
There is a question Christians sometimes hope nobody asks.
Because when someone finally does, the room can get uncomfortable.
“If marriage is supposed to be between one man and one woman, why did God allow men in the Old Testament to have multiple wives?”
Abraham had Sarah and Hagar.
Jacob married Leah and Rachel and also fathered children through Bilhah and Zilpah.
David had multiple wives.
Solomon had hundreds of wives and concubines.
And these are not obscure villains hiding in forgotten corners of Scripture.
These are some of the most recognizable names in the Bible.
So what are we supposed to do with that?
Pretend those passages are not there?
Explain them away?
Say, “Well, that was the Old Testament,” and quickly change the subject?
No.
Christian faith does not require us to be frightened by difficult passages.
We need to read them more carefully.
Because once you see what Scripture is actually doing, something remarkable happens.
The scandal does not disappear.
It becomes part of the story of grace.
And the answer begins somewhere many people never think to look.
Not with Abraham.
Not with Jacob.
Not with David.
Not with Solomon.
Before there was a king with a harem…
before there was a patriarch caught between two women…
before jealousy entered a tent…
before one household became divided between competing mothers and wounded children…
there was a garden.
And in that garden, God showed us the pattern before human sin complicated it.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
Look closely at the Hebrew ending:
וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
wehayu lebasar echad
“And they shall become one flesh.”
That final word, אֶחָד — ʾeḥāḏ, means “one.”
One flesh.
The biblical story does not begin with one man surrounded by wives.
It begins with Adam and Eve.
A man.
His wife.
A covenantal union expressed as one flesh.
That matters enormously, because one of the biggest mistakes we can make while reading Scripture is assuming that everything the Bible describes is something God prescribes.
The Bible describes murder.
That does not mean God approves of murder.
It describes adultery.
It does not bless adultery.
It describes drunkenness, deception, slavery, betrayal, incest, idolatry, war, abuse of power, and spectacular moral failure.
The Bible is brutally honest about humanity because the Bible is not propaganda for human goodness.
It is the story of a holy God dealing with fallen people.
And that distinction helps us understand polygamy.
More precisely, most of the biblical examples involve polygyny—one man having multiple wives—rather than the broader category of polygamy.
Scripture records it.
The Mosaic Law regulates circumstances arising within it.
But regulation is not the same thing as declaring something God’s original ideal.
That difference is enormous.
Imagine finding guardrails beside a dangerous mountain road.
The existence of the guardrails does not mean the government designed the cliff.
The guardrails exist because the cliff is already there and human lives need protection.
In a fallen world, biblical law sometimes restrains damage inside situations that are already far removed from Eden.
Consider Exodus 21:10, where a man who takes another wife is forbidden to deprive the first woman of essential marital provision.
Or consider Deuteronomy 21:15–17, which addresses inheritance when a man has two wives and favors one over the other.
The law is dealing with an existing human reality and limiting injustice within it.
It does not follow that God is saying, “This is My beautiful design for marriage.”
In fact, Scripture gives us another extraordinary clue in its instructions for Israel’s future kings.
Deuteronomy 17:17 says:
וְלֹא יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ נָשִׁים וְלֹא יָסוּר לְבָבוֹ
welōʾ yarbeh-lô nāšîm welōʾ yāsûr leḇāḇô
In essence:
“He shall not multiply wives for himself, lest his heart turn away.”
Notice that.
God does not tell Israel’s king to build the largest harem in the nation.
He warns him against multiplying wives.
And then centuries later Solomon practically becomes a living illustration of why the warning existed.
The tragedy is breathtaking.
The king famous for wisdom becomes foolish precisely where God had warned kings to be careful.
Solomon accumulates wives.
His affections become divided.
And eventually his heart turns.
What Deuteronomy warned about, Solomon’s life dramatized.
That should make us rethink the claim that the Old Testament casually celebrates polygamy.
Because when you actually follow these households through the story, the picture is often painful.
Look at Abraham.
God promised Abraham descendants.
Years passed.
Sarah remained barren.
The waiting became unbearable.
So Sarah gave Hagar to Abraham.
Genesis does not hide what happened next.
Pregnancy produced contempt.
Contempt produced jealousy.
Jealousy produced mistreatment.
Mistreatment drove Hagar into the wilderness.
Eventually Ishmael and Hagar were sent away.
What looked like a human solution to an impossible promise became a household soaked in tears.
Then look at Jacob.
He loved Rachel.
He was deceived into marrying Leah.
He then married Rachel too.
And suddenly we are watching two sisters competing for the affection of the same husband.
Leah desperately wants to be loved.
Rachel desperately wants children.
Children begin to carry the emotional weight of their mothers’ rivalry.
Servant women are brought into the reproductive struggle.
Names given to babies become windows into heartbreak, competition, vindication, and longing.
Read those chapters slowly and you stop seeing a glamorous ancient household.
You start hearing wounded people.
One woman whispering, in effect, “Maybe now my husband will love me.”
Another crying because she cannot conceive.
A husband trapped inside the consequences of deception and favoritism.
Children growing up inside a fractured family system.
The Bible does not need to interrupt every paragraph and say, “Polygyny creates problems.”
The story is showing you.
Then comes David.
A man after God’s own heart—and also a man capable of terrible sin.
David accumulated wives.
Then he saw Bathsheba.
She belonged to another man.
David already possessed what Uriah did not: multiple wives and royal power.
Yet power whispered the same ancient lie sin always whispers:
“You deserve more.”
David took Bathsheba.
Then he arranged Uriah’s death.
And when Nathan confronted him, the prophet exposed the ugliness of David’s entitlement.
This was never simply about sexual desire.
It was about a heart that stopped recognizing boundaries.
Then Solomon takes the pattern to catastrophic proportions.
Women become part of royal accumulation.
Political alliances become marriages.
Desire and power merge.
And eventually the king’s heart is pulled toward other gods.
The story moves from Eden’s “one flesh” toward a palace filled with divided affection.
And perhaps that is the deepest issue.
Because marriage in Scripture is not merely about sexuality.
It is about covenant.
Faithfulness.
Union.
Belonging.
Exclusive devotion.
And those themes eventually point beyond human marriage altogether.
But before we reach that point, we need to face the hardest part of the question.
Why would God tolerate arrangements that fell short of His original design?
Jesus gives us a principle that helps enormously.
When religious leaders questioned Him about divorce in Matthew 19, Jesus did something revealing.
He went backward.
Past Moses.
Past Israel.
Back to creation.
He quoted the Genesis pattern of male and female becoming one flesh.
When they objected by pointing to Moses’ allowance concerning divorce, Jesus answered with words that unlock far more than the divorce debate:
πρὸς τὴν σκληροκαρδίαν ὑμῶν
pros tēn sklērokardian hymōn
“Because of your hardness of heart…”
Then comes the crucial statement:
ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς δὲ οὐ γέγονεν οὕτως
ap’ archēs de ou gegonen houtōs
“But from the beginning it was not so.”
Do not miss that sentence.
Jesus teaches us that something can exist within Mosaic regulation without representing God’s creational ideal.
Why?
Because God was dealing with hard-hearted human beings.

That does not mean every Old Testament concession can automatically be treated identically. We should not force Jesus’ specific teaching about divorce into passages where He was not directly speaking about polygyny.
But the interpretive principle is unmistakable:
To understand God’s design, Jesus takes us back to the beginning.
And what do we find at the beginning?
Not Adam, Eve, Rachel, Leah, Bilhah, and Zilpah.
Adam and Eve.
One flesh.
God enters history not by waiting until humanity becomes morally perfect, but by meeting sinners inside the wreckage they have created and progressively moving His redemptive purposes forward.
That is what makes the Bible so painfully believable.
If human beings were inventing a religious propaganda book designed to make their heroes look magnificent, the Old Testament would be an extraordinarily strange way to do it.
Noah gets drunk.
Abraham lies.
Jacob deceives.
Moses loses his temper.
David commits adultery and orchestrates a killing.
Solomon’s wisdom does not save him from catastrophic compromise.
Peter denies Jesus.
The disciples argue about greatness.
The Bible refuses to airbrush its heroes.
Because they were never the Hero.
Jesus is.
That is where this question becomes much more personal than an argument about ancient marriage customs.
Because it is easy to stare at Solomon’s household and think:
“How could he let his heart become so divided?”
But perhaps the more uncomfortable question is:
How divided is yours?
Solomon multiplied wives.
Maybe you multiply secret identities.
One version of you worships on Sunday.
Another version lives online after midnight.
One version speaks about Jesus.
Another quietly feeds an addiction.
One version tells everyone the marriage is fine.
Another knows resentment has been poisoning the home for years.
One version posts Scripture.
Another cannot forgive.
One version says, “God is first.”
But money gets the first anxiety.
Sex gets the strongest appetite.
Approval gets the deepest craving.
Politics gets the loudest passion.
Entertainment gets the most time.
And Jesus gets whatever remains.
Different century.
Same divided heart.
That is why this cannot remain merely an article about “those polygamous people in the Old Testament.”
Scripture is holding up a mirror.
God warned the king not to multiply wives because his heart could turn away.
The issue underneath the visible behavior was the heart.
לְבָבוֹ — leḇāḇô.
His heart.
And perhaps somebody reading this has just realized:
“My heart has been turning too.”
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your spouse does not know.
Maybe your pastor does not know.
Maybe your children think you are stronger than you are.
And maybe you have become so good at carrying two versions of yourself that you almost forgot which one was real.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not God pretending your sin does not matter.
The Gospel is God doing something infinitely more costly.
He exposes sin…
and then provides a Savior.
The answer to human brokenness was never Abraham.
Never Jacob.
Never David.
Never Solomon.
Every one of them needed mercy.
Every one of them pointed beyond himself.
Then Jesus came.
And unlike every compromised king before Him, Christ remained faithful.
Where Adam failed, Christ obeyed.
Where Israel wandered, Christ remained faithful.
Where kings accumulated power for themselves, Jesus emptied Himself and took the form of a servant.
Where David took another man’s bride and sent the husband toward death, Jesus moves in the opposite direction:
Christ gives Himself to death to rescue His Bride.
Do you see how beautiful the reversal is?
Sin says:
“Take.”
Jesus says:
“I give Myself.”
Sin consumes.
Jesus sacrifices.
Sin uses people.
Jesus lays down His life for people.
Sin divides.
Jesus reconciles.
Sin stains.
Jesus cleanses.
And suddenly marriage becomes even larger than Genesis.
Paul writes in Ephesians 5 about husband and wife, then unveils the mystery:
marriage ultimately points toward Christ and the Church.
Jesus is the faithful Bridegroom.
And His covenant faithfulness is not fragile.
He does not abandon His people because another bride catches His attention.
He does not become bored with His covenant.
He does not wake up one morning and decide His Bride has become inconvenient.
He loves.
He gives Himself.
He sanctifies.
He cleanses.
He keeps His promises.
That is why biblical faithfulness matters.
Human marriage was always meant to tell a larger story.
And this is also why the Bible’s record of polygyny should never become ammunition for mocking people who lived within those broken arrangements.
Especially women.
Hagar was not a theological problem to God.
She was a suffering woman whom God saw in the wilderness.
Leah was not merely “the unwanted wife.”
God saw that she was unloved.
Bathsheba was not merely a footnote in David’s biography.
The biblical story ultimately places her within the genealogy leading toward Christ.
Again and again, God walks into stories human beings have complicated beyond recognition…
and grace starts rewriting them.
That does not make the sin good.
Grace never needs evil to become good in order to redeem people from it.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
The crucifixion of Jesus was an act of horrifying human injustice.
And God turned humanity’s darkest act into the place where redemption was accomplished.
That is what God does.
He does not call darkness light.
He enters darkness carrying resurrection.
Maybe that is why this subject matters more than you thought.
You came here asking:
“Why did God allow polygamy?”
But perhaps underneath that question is another one.
“Why does God tolerate broken people at all?”
Why Abraham?
Why Jacob?
Why David?
Why Solomon?
Why Peter?
Why me?
And there it is.
The question has finally reached your own front door.
Because if God only worked through people whose lives perfectly reflected His design, the Bible would become very short.
And so would the Church.
We are all people standing somewhere between what God designed and what sin has damaged.
Some damage is visible.
Some is hidden behind church clothes and carefully selected photographs.
Some people have broken marriages.
Some have broken sexuality.
Some have broken trust.
Some have broken families.
Some have addictions they promised God they would quit a hundred times.
Some are carrying consequences that cannot simply be reversed.
And Christianity does not announce:
“Fix your history, and then Jesus might accept you.”
Christianity announces:
Christ came for sinners.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Come into the light.
Receive mercy.
And then follow Him.
Grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
Grace is the power and pardon that meet us in our guilt and begin transforming us.
That is why Jesus’ words are so powerful:
“From the beginning it was not so.”
Jesus does not merely expose how far humanity wandered.
He points us toward restoration.
Toward God’s intention.
Toward faithfulness.
Toward holiness.
Toward hearts no longer divided between God and idols.
And ultimately toward the new creation, where everything sin fractured will finally be placed beneath the reign of Christ.
So did God “allow” polygyny in the Old Testament?
Yes, in the sense that He dealt with people living within societies where it existed and gave laws addressing and restraining circumstances created by it.
But do not confuse divine toleration and regulation in a fallen world with the declaration of a creational ideal.
Scripture begins with one man and one woman becoming one flesh.
It warns Israel’s king against multiplying wives.
It repeatedly shows the jealousy, rivalry, exploitation, favoritism, family conflict, and spiritual danger surrounding plural marriages.
And when Jesus is asked about marriage and divorce, He directs His hearers back beyond later concessions:
to the beginning.
That is the biblical trajectory.
Creation.
Fall.
Human hardness.
Divine restraint.
Promise.
Redemption.
Christ.
Restoration.
And maybe now you understand why the Bible leaves the scandals in.
God could have given us sanitized heroes.
Instead, He gave us Abraham’s household.
Jacob’s rivalry.
David’s collapse.
Solomon’s divided heart.
Why?
Because Scripture is not telling us how impressive humanity is.
Scripture is telling us how desperately humanity needs Jesus Christ.
And perhaps that is exactly what somebody you know needs to hear today.
Not another polished Christian pretending the Bible has no difficult passages.
Not another believer frightened by hard questions.
But someone willing to open Scripture, face the scandal honestly, and still discover that Christ stands at the center of the story.
Not merely because you agree with it.
Be honest.
Somebody reading your three words may realize they are not the only person fighting their way back toward the light.
Because difficult questions return.
And when they do, you need more than a slogan.
You need Scripture.
It does not.
Not because giving money purchases blessing, salvation, forgiveness, or spiritual status.
It cannot.
Jesus purchased our redemption—not us.
But one genuine way believers can glorify God is by willingly using what He has entrusted to them to support faithful Gospel work and help truth reach other people.
And there is more.
Come to Jesus.
Not to a brand.
Not to merchandise.
Not to a page.
To Christ.
Repent of sin.
Trust the crucified and risen Savior.
Bring Him the divided heart.
Bring Him the secret chapter.
Bring Him the marriage wounds.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the questions you were afraid Christians would not let you ask.
The Bible is filled with scandal because humanity is filled with sinners.
But the Bible does not end with scandal.
It moves toward a wedding.
Toward Christ and His redeemed people.
Toward a Bridegroom who never betrays His Bride.
Toward a King whose heart never turns away.
Toward the Lamb who was slain.
Toward resurrection.
Toward restoration.
Toward grace.
And perhaps the most unforgettable truth hiding inside all those broken Old Testament households is this:
God did not preserve their scandals so you would imitate their brokenness; He preserved them so you would recognize your need for the faithful Savior they could never be.
Share that truth.
Because the names change.
The centuries change.
The scandals change.
But humanity still needs the same Savior.
And when sin has written a chapter that looks impossible to redeem, never forget who is holding the pen.
